newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SE Asia grain/oilseeds market in small-lot buying.
newsitem.headline: SE Asia grain/oilseeds market in small-lot buying.

text.p: Southeast Asian grain and oilseeds buyers are buying small lots while demand for Indian-origin soymeal remains firm, traders said on Thursday.
"The Malaysians and Indonesians are buying chunks here and there. Business in Southeast Asia is chugging along," a trader in a Western commodity house said.
"There's a lot of small-lot buying going at the moment, especially for soymeal," another trader said.

Indonesia, which recently bought between 70,000 to 90,000 tonnes of soymeal, purchased an additional 20,000 tonnes of Indian-origin soymeal at a price of about $315-$318 a tonne C&F for November/December shipment, traders said.

Dealers said Malaysia bought about 10,000 tonnes of corn from Vietnam for prompt shipment at around $175-$180 a tonne C&F. Malaysian buyers were also said to have bought about 20,000 tonnes of wheat, but other details on that purchase were not available.
The Malaysians were also reported to be seeking 20,000 tonnes of soymeal after recently buying 30,000 tonnes, the dealers said.
"There is good underlying demand in the market. Our impression is that coverage on the deferred months remains insufficient," one grains analyst said.

Traders said Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia would be keen to put on some coverage for soymeal in the early part of 1997. Malaysia and Indonesia may still need about 100,000 tonnes of soymeal each, while Thailand could be in the market for 150,000 tonnes, dealers said.

Indian new crop soymeal is quoted in Southeast Asia at around $320-$325 a tonne C&F for November/December shipment against about $315-$320 a tonne last week, mainly on the back of strong demand, dealers said.
Old crop Indian soymeal was quoted at about $340-$345 a tonne C&F against $330-$335 a tonne last week, Singapore-based traders said.
In the United States, the September soymeal futures contract on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) closed on Wednesday $1.10 a tonne up at $274.90 a tonne.
Corn demand in the region remained thin since most countries are well-covered for their needs through to year-end and will only buy small parcels for early 1997, dealers said.
Prices of U.S. corn in Southeast Asia were quoted in a range of $161-$163 a tonne C&F for November/December shipment on a Panamax vessel against $167-$172 a tonne C&F last week.
The price of September corn in Chicago rose U.S. 4-1/4 cents to end on Wednesday at $3.55-1/2 a bushel.
Regional traders were watching the U.S. weather market over fears of a frost hitting the crop and monitoring the availability of Argentine corn for buyers in the region.
"Nobody is going out to buy four cargoes of corn despite the current low prices like what the South Koreans did a few weeks ago," one trader said.
The South Koreans bought nearly 1.5 million tonnes of corn a few weeks ago to take advantage of falling prices in Chicago.
"I just don't see anybody being aggressive," a grains trader added. "It should be pretty much hand-to-mouth for now."
